chapters.title: Chapter 7: Parents, Teachers, and Coaches: Where Do Mindsets Come From?

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Praise: Intelligence, Process, and Speed Messages
assets.visual_frame_description: A family dinner table in a bright Denver kitchen. Nine-year-old Maya beams as she tells her mom, aunts, and uncle that she got an A on a spelling test without studying. Adults in the scene respond with different kinds of praise. A split-panel classifier on the screen sorts each praise statement into one of three labeled columns as the player watches.
assets.player_mission: Listen to each praise statement the adults make at Maya's dinner and decide which column it belongs in: intelligence/talent praise, process/strategy praise, or speed/perfection praise. Place the statements correctly to expose how the same moment can send either a fixed-mindset or a growth-minded message.
key_concepts: Praising children's intelligence or talent sends a fixed-mindset message that judges permanent traits rather than development.
Dweck's seven experiments with hundreds of children found that praising children's intelligence harms their motivation and harms their performance.
Children who are praised for being smart hear a hidden message: if I don't learn something quickly, I'm not smart.
Praise that focuses on speed and perfection tells children that fast, flawless work is what earns admiration.
Speed and perfection are the enemy of difficult learning, because children reason that if they are smart only when fast and perfect, they should avoid challenges.
Process praise focuses on what children accomplished through practice, study, persistence, and good strategies.
Praising intelligence gives children a boost only for the moment; the minute they hit a snag, their confidence goes out the window and their motivation hits rock bottom.
If success means you're smart, then failure means you're dumb, which is the fixed mindset.
The best gift parents can give children is to teach them to love challenges, be intrigued by mistakes, enjoy effort, seek new strategies, and keep on learning.
When a task is completed too quickly and perfectly, Dweck suggests saying the task was too easy and finding something the child can really learn from.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests how the content of praise communicates mindset: praising intelligence or talent signals that fixed traits are being judged, while process praise signals that abilities develop through effort and strategy. Dweck reports that after seven experiments with hundreds of children, praising children's intelligence harmed both their motivation and their performance.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: At dinner, Maya's mom says, "You're so brilliant, you got an A without even studying!" In which column does this statement belong, given how Dweck analyzes praise?

rows.label: Maya's mom says, "You're so brilliant, you got an A without even studying!"
Her aunt tells her cousin, "You're such a natural athlete," during a backyard game.
Her dad says, "Wow, you did that so quickly!" as she races through her math sheet.
Her uncle says, "Look, you didn't make any mistakes!" inspecting her spelling test.
Her teacher says, "I like the way you tried all kinds of strategies on that math problem until you finally got it."
Her grandmother says, "You really studied for your test and your improvement shows it. You read the material over, outlined it, and tested yourself."

distractors: It belongs in the process column because it mentions how she did on the test.
It belongs in the speed column because she finished without studying.
It belongs in no column because praise is always supportive for children.
assets.explanation: Dweck's praise research shows that "You're so brilliant, you got an A without even studying!" praises the child's intelligence and implies that effortless success proves a fixed trait. The child hears, "If I don't learn something quickly, I'm not smart," which makes her avoid hard work. Process praise ("you tried strategies," "you studied and outlined and tested yourself") and speed/perfection praise ("so quickly," "no mistakes") are separate categories, with speed and perfection flagged as the enemy of difficult learning.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Process Praise After a Strong Test Performance
assets.visual_frame_description: A Friday evening in the Rivera family kitchen in Austin, Texas. Twelve-year-old Sofia bursts through the door waving a test paper and announces her score to her mother, Elena. Warm lamplight, a stack of dishes, and Sofia's glowing face set the scene as Elena decides how to respond to the news.
assets.player_mission: Choose Elena's response to Sofia's high test score. Your goal is to reinforce a growth mindset by praising the process that led to the result without deflating Sofia's excitement, and to avoid trait or speed praise that would make her afraid of hard tasks.
key_concepts: Praising children's intelligence harms their motivation and their performance, according to Dweck's seven experiments with hundreds of children.
Process praise celebrates what a child accomplished through practice, study, persistence, and good strategies.
Asking children about their work shows interest in their efforts and choices and recognizes how they improved.
Children love praise, but the boost from intelligence praise lasts only until they hit a snag.
Growth-minded praise ties the process to the outcome, so children see that engaging in the process helped them learn.
Haim Ginott concluded that praise should deal not with the child's personality attributes but with his efforts and achievements.
Parents can appreciate their children enthusiastically as long as they keep away from praise that judges intelligence or talent.
A student in the chapter asked her 12-year-old sister about the effort she put into studying and how she improved from the year before.
Speed and perfection are the enemy of difficult learning, because children reason that if they are smart when fast and perfect, they'd better not take on anything challenging.
Parents who want to give children a gift should teach them to love challenges, be intrigued by mistakes, enjoy effort, seek new strategies, and keep on learning.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests process praise: children infer from praise whether their abilities are fixed traits being judged or skills that grow through effort and strategy. Dweck reports that process praise, naming the study, strategies, and persistence that led to learning, is what moves children toward a growth mindset, while intelligence praise makes their confidence and motivation fragile.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.scenario_setup: Sofia scored 102 on her social studies test and repeats the news about five times over the weekend. Last year her grades dropped lower and lower as the year went on. Elena remembers a lesson about praise and wants to respond in a way that builds a growth mindset. The stakes: how Elena reacts will shape whether Sofia studies to learn or to prove she is smart.
assets.dialogue:
SOFIA: Mom! I got 102 on my social studies test. Did you hear me? One hundred and two!
ELENA: I heard you, honey, and I can see you're bursting about it. Tell me more.
SOFIA: I studied the chapter like three times, made flashcards of the dates, and last year my grades kept dropping. This time it finally stuck!
ELENA: That's a real change from last year. What do you think you did differently this time?
SOFIA: I didn't just read it once. I outlined it, and I quizzed myself out loud.
ELENA: So the outlining and quizzing really worked for you. How does it feel to see that pay off?
SOFIA: It feels like I actually understand it now. Can I try that for science too?
ELENA: That sounds like a great plan. I'm proud of how you stuck with it and kept learning.
choices: You're so brilliant! You got 102 without even trying hard. I knew you had it in you.
Wow, that was fast! You finished it so quickly, you must be a genius at social studies.
I'm so proud of how you studied, how you outlined it and quizzed yourself, and your improvement really shows it. What do you think helped the most?
A 102? Not bad. Now let's see you keep that up so you stay ahead of everyone else.
assets.theoretical_principle: Process praise (praise for the process children engage in: hard work, strategies, focus, and perseverance) tied to the child's learning and improvement.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Option 2 follows Dweck's advice to praise the growth-oriented process and tie it to the child's learning and improvement; it is modeled on the chapter's student who asked her 12-year-old sister about the effort she put in and how she improved from the year before. Options 0 and 1 praise intelligence and speed respectively, and both signal that quick, effortless success is what earns admiration, making Sofia reluctant to take on hard tasks. Option 3 attaches approval to the grade itself, setting up the fixed-mindset trap of proving worth through performance.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Messages About Failure: Elizabeth's Gymnastics Meet
assets.visual_frame_description: In a Portland, Oregon gym, ten-year-old Becca sits slumped on the bleachers after the district meet, eyes red, clutching an empty gym bag. She competed first in floor exercises and lost as the scoring changed, finishing the night without a single ribbon. Her father, Marcus, crouches beside her as the crowd files out.
assets.player_mission: Choose Marcus's response to Becca's disappointment. Your goal is to sympathize with her feelings while telling her the truth and giving her a path to improve, instead of offering an insincere boost, blaming the judges, devaluing the sport, or promising that ability alone will win next time.
key_concepts: The societal message that parents must protect children from failure can be harmful in the long run.
Telling a child she was the best when she was not is insincere and offers no recipe for recovery or improvement.
Blaming the judges teaches children to blame others for their deficiencies.
Devaluing an activity a child loses at teaches her to devalue things she doesn't do well in right away.
Reassuring a child that she has the ability to win next time is dangerous, because ability does not automatically take you where you want to go.
Elizabeth's growth-minded father sympathized with her disappointment, told her the truth, and taught her how to learn from her failures.
Elizabeth responded by spending much more time repeating and perfecting her routines, especially the ones she was weakest in.
At the next meet Elizabeth won five ribbons for the individual events and was the overall champion.
Children need honest and constructive feedback; if they are protected from it, they won't learn well.
Withholding constructive criticism does not help children's confidence; it harms their future.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests messages about failure: growth-minded parents sympathize with disappointment but give honest feedback plus a path to improvement, whereas fixed-minded responses either devalue the activity, blame others, or hand out a phony "you have the ability" boost. Dweck reports that Elizabeth's father's honest response taught her to learn from failure, and she went on to win five ribbons and the overall championship at her next meet.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.scenario_setup: Becca loves gymnastics and felt confident, even imagining where she would hang her first ribbon. After the meet she is devastated. Marcus has read about Elizabeth in Dweck's book and knows this is a messages-about-failure moment. The stakes: his words will either teach her how to recover from failure or teach her to avoid, blame, or devalue it.
assets.dialogue:
BECCA: I didn't get any ribbons, Dad. Not one. I practiced the floor routine so much.
MARCUS: I know, sweetheart. I know how it feels to have your hopes up, to give it your best, and still not win.
BECCA: The judges changed the scoring after I went first. It wasn't fair.
MARCUS: That part was out of your hands. But let's talk about what you can control.
BECCA: I guess I could work on my weakest events. The beam was really shaky.
MARCUS: If gymnastics is something you really want to excel in, that's what it will take, more work. If you want to do it just for fun, that's fine too.
BECCA: I want to win next time. Will you help me practice more?
MARCUS: I'd love to. Let's make a plan for the routines you struggled with.
choices: You were robbed. Those judges had it wrong, that ribbon was rightfully yours.
You were the best out there, Becca. I don't care what the scores said.
Gymnastics isn't that important, honey. And you have the ability, so you'll surely win next time.

I know you're disappointed, and I'm sorry. But you haven't really earned it yet, some of those girls have trained longer and harder. If it's what you really want, you'll have to work for it, and I'll help you.
assets.theoretical_principle: Honest, growth-minded feedback on failure: sympathize with the child's disappointment, tell the truth, and give a recipe for improvement instead of protecting the child from failure.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Option 3 mirrors what Elizabeth's growth-minded father actually said: he sympathized with her disappointment but told her the truth and taught her how to learn from the loss, and she responded by spending far more time perfecting her routines, especially her weakest ones, and winning five ribbons plus the overall title at her next meet. Option 0 places blame on the judges when the problem was mostly her performance. Option 1 is insincere, since she knows she was not the best, and offers no recipe for recovery. Option 2 devalues the sport and reassures her about ability, which is dangerous because ability does not automatically take you where you want to go.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A quiet Chicago suburban living room the night before the College Board tests. Kristina, a bright high school senior, paces by the window, wringing her hands. Her parents, Dan and Priya, sit on the couch, watching her and deciding how to build her confidence for the morning.
assets.player_mission: Choose what Dan and Priya say to Kristina the night before the test. Your goal is to lower the stakes by removing the feeling that she is being evaluated, rather than reassuring her about her intelligence, which would raise the stakes even higher.
key_concepts: Reassuring children about their intelligence or talent before a test backfires and makes them more afraid to show a deficiency.
Kristina studied and knew the material, but her anxiety made her mind go blank on tests and her grades suffered.
The supportive message "you know how smart you are, you've got this nailed" raises the stakes even higher.
The recommended message is: we are not evaluating you; we care about your learning, and we know that you've learned your stuff.
Praising or reassuring about intelligence turns every performance into a test of permanent worth.
Growth-minded reassurance emphasizes learning and the process, not the outcome.
Children are remarkably sensitive to the messages behind their parents' words.

Every word and action can send a fixed-mindset message (you have permanent traits and I'm judging them) or a growth-mindset message (you are a developing person and I'm committed to your development).
Fixed-mindset children interpret parental help as an attempt to measure how smart they are.
Growth-minded children interpret parental help as encouragement to learn and study better in the future.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests the backfire effect of intelligence reassurance: telling a test-anxious child she is smart raises the stakes because it implies her fixed trait is being judged. Dweck's recommendation is non-evaluative reassurance that focuses on care for learning, which the book illustrates through the high school student Kristina whose mind went blank on tests.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.scenario_setup: Kristina always studies and always knows the material, but on test day her anxiety makes her mind go blank and her grades suffer. The schools she longs to attend prize these tests highly. Her parents want to help her feel secure. The stakes: their reassurance will either raise the stakes higher or remove the feeling that she is being evaluated.
assets.dialogue:
KRISTINA: I know everything, but my mind always goes blank. What if it happens tomorrow?
DAN: Look, you know how smart you are and we know how smart you are. You've got this nailed. Now stop worrying.
KRISTINA: That's what you said before the last one, and I still froze.
PRIYA: It must be a terrible thing to feel like everyone is evaluating you and you can't show what you know.
KRISTINA: It is. I feel like my whole worth is on the line.
PRIYA: We want you to know that we are not evaluating you. We care about your learning, and we know that you have learned your stuff.
DAN: And we're proud that you've stuck to it and kept learning all year.
KRISTINA: So even if I freeze tomorrow, you won't think less of me?
PRIYA: No. We care about your learning, not a score. And let's make a plan for what to do if you feel yourself tensing up.
choices: Stop worrying. You're one of the smartest kids in the school, you've got this nailed.
If you don't do well, it's the test's fault, not yours. The College Board is a rigged system anyway.

We are not evaluating you. We care about your learning, we know you've learned your material, and we're proud that you've stuck to it and kept learning. Now let's plan what to do if your mind goes blank.
Tests don't matter at all in the long run, honey. Just relax and get a good night's sleep.
assets.theoretical_principle: Reassurance about intelligence or talent backfires; non-evaluative reassurance that focuses on care for learning and the process reduces the stakes.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Option 2 follows the book's recommended message: acknowledge her fear of evaluation, explicitly say you are not evaluating her, emphasize care for her learning, and move to a practical coping plan. Option 0 is trait reassurance, and it raises the stakes by implying her smartness is on trial, exactly what made Kristina's grades suffer. Option 1 removes all responsibility and gives her no way to manage the test. Option 3 devalues the test and dodges her real worry. Reassuring children about their intelligence or talent backfires because it makes them more afraid to show a deficiency.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A Baltimore apartment kitchen table at 6 p.m. Twelve-year-old Billy hands his father, Tom, a homework sheet completed in a rush, with several questions skipped and the rest answered in short, sloppy sentences. Tom sets down his coffee and studies the page, visibly frustrated and disappointed.
assets.player_mission: Choose Tom's response to Billy's rushed homework. Your goal is to deliver constructive criticism that helps Billy fix the work and learn, not judgment that questions his intelligence and character.
key_concepts: Constructive criticism means helping the child fix something, build a better product, or do a better job, not judging the child.
Feedback like "you are either dense or irresponsible" questions a child's intelligence and character and implies the defects are permanent.
An alternative response is: "Son, it really makes me upset when you don't do a full job. When do you think you can complete this?"
Another alternative is: "Is there something you didn't understand in the assignment? Would you like me to go over it with you?"
Ginott's story of Philip shows children can be taught to separate the event from a label: "The nails spilled, I'll pick them up!"
Children who are protected from constructive feedback won't learn well and will experience advice, coaching, and feedback as negative and undermining.
Withholding constructive criticism does not help children's confidence; it harms their future.
Children are ready to judge and label themselves, and adults can teach them not to.
Growth-minded discipline asks: what message am I sending, I will judge and punish you, or I will help you think and learn?
Growth-minded parents set high standards but teach children how to reach them; they say no as a fair, thoughtful, respectful no.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests the difference between constructive and judgmental criticism: judgmental feedback labels the child's permanent traits, while constructive feedback tells the child how to fix the work. The book contrasts the father who called his son "dense or irresponsible" with process-oriented alternatives that express upset, check understanding, and schedule completion.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.scenario_setup: Billy rushed through his homework, skipping questions and answering the rest sloppily. Tom is frustrated, but he remembers the chapter's point that constructive means helping the child fix something, build a better product, or do a better job. The stakes: his words will either teach Billy how to do better or label him as permanently flawed.
assets.dialogue:
TOM: Billy, can we look at this homework together?
BILLY: I did it. Can I go play now?
TOM: You rushed through it, skipped questions, and the answers are pretty short. It makes me upset when you don't do a full job.
BILLY: I didn't like the assignment.
TOM: Is there something you didn't understand in the assignment? Would you like me to go over it with you?
BILLY: Maybe the third question. I guessed on that one.
TOM: Let's look at it together, then. When do you think you can complete the rest, tonight or tomorrow?
BILLY: Tonight, I guess. If we figure out the third one, the rest are easy.
TOM: Good. I feel sad when I see you missing a chance to learn, so let's make sure this one counts.
choices: This is your homework? Can't you ever get it right? You are either dense or irresponsible, which is it?
It's fine, don't worry about it. I'll just do the rest of it for you so you can go play.
Son, it really upsets me when you don't do a full job. When do you think you can complete this? And is there something you didn't understand that I could go over with you?
Your teacher gave you a boring assignment and way too much of it. I'll call the school about that.
assets.theoretical_principle: Constructive criticism (feedback that helps the child fix something, build a better product, or do a better job) versus judgmental criticism that questions intelligence and character.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Option 2 uses the alternatives the book offers Billy's father: express the upset, ask when the work can be completed, and offer to go over anything he didn't understand. Option 0 is the book's example of what the angry father actually said, questioning the boy's intelligence and character and implying the defects were permanent. Option 1 removes all responsibility and teaches Billy nothing. Option 3 blames the teacher, mirroring parents who heap blame on coaches and referees instead of giving the child honest, constructive feedback.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Failure Response Taxonomy: Sympathy, Protection, Blame
assets.visual_frame_description: A classified dashboard displays a young gymnast on a podium that keeps moving out of reach. Beside the image, five parents' voices float in speech bubbles over the bleachers, each reacting to a child who just lost a meet. A three-column sorter awaits each reaction.
assets.player_mission: Sort each reaction to the child's loss into the correct column: growth-minded failure message, self-esteem-protective message, or blame-shifting message. Classify every reaction correctly to reveal which responses help a child learn from failure.
key_concepts: The strongest societal message about boosting children's self-esteem is to protect them from failure, which can be harmful in the long run.
Telling a child she was the best is insincere when she was not, and it offers no recipe for how to recover or how to improve.
Telling a child she was robbed places blame on others when the problem was mostly her performance.
Reassuring a child that an activity isn't important teaches her to devalue things she doesn't do well in right away.
Telling a child she has the ability and will surely win next time is dangerous, because ability does not automatically take you where you want to go.
Elizabeth's growth-minded father told her the truth and taught her how to learn from her failures and do what it takes to succeed in the future.
Elizabeth responded by spending much more time repeating and perfecting her routines, especially the ones she was weakest in.
At the next meet Elizabeth won five ribbons for the individual events and was the overall champion of the competition.
Coaches report that athletes now grumble that corrective feedback undermines their confidence, while parents on the ride home heap blame on coaches and referees.
Withholding constructive criticism does not help children's confidence; it harms their future.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix sorts reactions to a child's failure into growth-minded honesty, protective self-esteem boosting, and blame-shifting responses. Dweck argues that the societal protect-them-from-failure message is harmful in the long run, and that honest, sympathetic feedback, as Elizabeth's father gave, teaches children how to recover and improve.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: After Becca loses her gymnastics meet, her father says, "You haven't really earned it yet, some girls have trained longer and worked harder. If this is something you really want, you'll have to work for it." In which column does this response belong?
assets.column_a_label: Growth-minded failure message (sympathy plus honest feedback and a path to improve)
assets.column_b_label: Self-esteem-protective message (shield the child from failure)

rows.label: "You haven't really earned it yet, you'll have to work for it," while sympathizing with the disappointment.
Tell the child you thought she was the best, even though she was not.
Reassure her that gymnastics is not that important.
Tell her she has the ability and will surely win next time.
Tell her she was robbed of a ribbon that was rightfully hers.
Let her know that if she wants gymnastics purely for fun that is fine, but if she wants to excel in competitions, more is required.

distractors: It belongs in the blame column because the father is blaming the other girls for winning.
It belongs in the protective column because the father is sparing the child's feelings.
It belongs in no column because parents should never mention a child's failure.
assets.explanation: Elizabeth's father sympathized with her disappointment but told her the truth and gave her a recipe for improvement, which is the growth-minded failure message in column a. "She was the best" and "she has the ability to win next time" are protective messages that are insincere or imply ability alone guarantees success. "She was robbed" places blame on the judges when the problem was mostly her performance. Elizabeth acted on her father's honest feedback, spent far more time perfecting her weakest routines, and became the overall champion at her next meet.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: False Growth Mindset: Effort Praise as a Consolation Prize
assets.visual_frame_description: A fifth-grade math classroom in a Newark school, after a worksheet is collected. Marcus, a student who has tried hard all month on fractions, stares at a paper full of wrong answers while Ms. Okonkwo, who attended a growth-mindset workshop, considers how to respond without discouraging him.
assets.player_mission: Choose Ms. Okonkwo's response to Marcus, who worked hard but shows almost no progress on fractions. Your goal is to respect his genuine effort while refusing to settle for effort that is not producing learning, and to steer him toward new strategies and help.
key_concepts: A false growth mindset can appear when adults praise effort that is not there, so the process praise has nothing real to reward.
Effort praise used as a consolation prize when kids are not learning is a major concern for Dweck.
We should never be content with effort that is not yielding further benefits; we need to figure out why the effort is not effective.
The process to be appreciated includes more than effort: hard work, trying new strategies, and seeking input from others.
We don't want children to just try harder with the same ineffective strategy.
Dweck fears the mindset concept will be used to make kids feel good when they're not learning, like the failed self-esteem movement.
"You can do anything" is empty reassurance unless children are given the skills and resources to make progress.
Growth-minded teaching means telling the truth and giving tools to close the gap, as Marva Collins told a student his reading score so they could work on it.
When math teachers teach for conceptual understanding, give feedback that deepens understanding, and allow revision, their students move toward a growth mindset in math.
Teachers can say "growth mindset" while using methods that do not foster it; it is their actions that matter.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests the false growth mindset: real growth-minded teaching does not settle for effort praise when learning is not happening, but diagnoses why effort fails and guides students toward new strategies and help. Dweck distinguishes the genuine process, hard work, trying new strategies, and seeking input, from effort used as a consolation prize, warning that the latter repeats the failures of the self-esteem movement.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.scenario_setup: Marcus has tried hard on fractions for a month with almost no progress, and today's worksheet is mostly wrong. Ms. Okonkwo is tempted to praise his effort so he won't feel bad, but she has also read the chapter's warning about the false growth mindset. The stakes: whether she treats effort as the goal or digs into why his effort is not producing learning.
assets.dialogue:
MS. OKONKWO: Marcus, I can see you really put in the time on this worksheet. That's real effort.
MARCUS: I tried, but I still don't get fractions. I guess I'm just not a math kid.
MS. OKONKWO: Let's not decide that today. Let's figure out where it's breaking down.
MARCUS: I keep doing what you showed me, the same way, and it comes out wrong.
MS. OKONKWO: So the strategy you're using isn't working. We don't want to just try harder with the same strategy. What did you do on this problem here?
MARCUS: I subtracted the denominators, like I always do.
MS. OKONKWO: That's the piece to fix. Let's try drawing the pieces on paper instead, and I'll check in with you before you move on.
MARCUS: Okay. If I use pictures, will it count?
MS. OKONKWO: It will count, because it will help you learn it. Effort is great, but our goal is for you to understand fractions. When you get it, we'll know the process worked.
choices: Nice effort, Marcus. That's what matters most, keep trying hard and you'll get it eventually.
You're just not a math person yet, but don't worry, everyone has their own strengths.

Your effort is real, but it's not getting you to learning yet, and I won't pretend otherwise. Let's change strategies, I'll show you how to draw the fractions, and we'll check that you understand before moving on.
You can do anything you set your mind to, Marcus. Believe in yourself and it will happen.
assets.theoretical_principle: Effort alone is not the growth mindset: the process includes trying new strategies and seeking help, and effort praise must never become a consolation prize when kids are not learning.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Option 2 follows the chapter's core correction to the false growth mindset: appreciate real effort, but never be content with effort that yields no further benefits, and instead figure out why the effort is ineffective and guide the student toward new strategies and resources. Option 0 is effort praise as a consolation prize, which Dweck says is like the failed self-esteem movement, making kids feel good when they are not learning. Option 1 labels Marcus with a fixed trait. Option 3 is the empty "you can do anything" reassurance that puts the onus on the student without giving skills or resources.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Coaching Philosophies: Knight, Wooden, and Summitt
assets.visual_frame_description: A sports-documentary control room with three large screens: one shows a furious coach berating a player in a locker room, one shows a quiet coach turning out gym lights, and one shows a champion team being routed on its home court. A three-column sorter labels each scene by coaching philosophy.
assets.player_mission: Sort each coaching behavior into the correct column: fixed-minded intimidation coaching, growth-minded preparation coaching, or success-infected complacency. Classify every scene correctly to distinguish how mindsets play out in the coaches' decisions.
key_concepts: Bobby Knight motivated his players not through respect for them but through intimidation, through fear of his judgments and explosions.
Knight's Holy Grail was the mistake-free game, and he was incapable of accepting failure because coaching gave him his identity.
Knight had a fixed mindset about himself and his coaching ability, so his team had to prove his ability every time out.
Knight won three championship teams, but at other times players and the team as a whole broke down, and players escaped by transferring or going early to the pros.
John Wooden asked not "Did I win? Did I lose?" but "Did I make my best effort?", and he coached that if so, "You may be outscored but you will never lose."
Wooden did not tolerate coasting; when players coasted in practice he turned out the lights and said, "Gentlemen, practice is over."
Wooden gave equal time and attention to all players regardless of initial skills, and unheralded recruits blossomed into starters.
Wooden refused to have any player's number retired while he coached, because the jersey and the number never belong to just one single player.
Pat Summitt found that success was the enemy: "Success lulls you. It makes the most ambitious of us complacent and sloppy."
Pat Riley called the same complacency the "disease of me," thinking you are the success and chucking the discipline that got you there.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix contrasts three coaching stances: fixed-minded intimidation that demands mistake-free games (Knight), growth-minded coaching that asks for full effort and develops every player (Wooden), and success-infection complacency that lulls teams into sloppiness (Summitt and Riley). Dweck argues that the fixed coach's judgment and fear can produce championships but also collapse and escape, while the growth coach's preparation and equal treatment develops players for life.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: A coach's players ask him, "Coach, did we win tonight?" He replies, "Did I make my best effort? That's the correct question." To which column does this coach belong?
assets.column_b_label: Growth-mindset coach (full preparation, full effort, equal treatment)

rows.label: A coach's Holy Grail is the mistake-free game and players are demeaned for losing (Bobby Knight).
A coach turns out the practice lights when players coast and says, "Gentlemen, practice is over" (John Wooden).
A coach says, "You may be outscored but you will never lose," if you made your best effort (John Wooden).
A team that just won the championship stops working and gets crushed at home by Stanford (Tennessee after 1996).
A coach leaves a Tampax in a player's locker to make a point about toughness (Bobby Knight).
A coach promises a backup to Bill Walton a pro contract, develops him, and he becomes rookie of the year (John Wooden).

distractors: The best-effort question belongs to the fixed coach who demands mistake-free perfection.
It belongs to the success-infected coach who lulls players into complacency.
No real coach would ever ask this question; it is only a slogan.
assets.explanation: The "Did I make my best effort?" question is John Wooden's, the straight-ahead growth-minded coach who asked for full preparation and full effort rather than mistake-free games. Knight's Holy Grail was the mistake-free game and he motivated through intimidation and fear, while Tennessee's post-championship complacency, what Pat Summitt called "success lulls you" and Pat Riley called the "disease of me," is the success-infection pattern. Wooden also gave equal time to all players and developed them, exemplified by the backup who became rookie of the year.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Boss Battle: Bobby Knight and the Fixed-Mindset Coach
assets.visual_frame_description: The scene is Assembly Hall, Indiana, during the "season on the brink." A dark locker room door swings open and Coach Knight, red-faced, berates Daryl Thomas, a big, fast player coaches call a "million dollar body," delivering a three-year assessment in front of the team. Steve Alford sits silently; the air is heavy with fear and judgment.
assets.player_mission: Defeat the fixed-mindset boss by first diagnosing why Knight explodes at his own players after a loss, then choosing a coaching intervention that can reach a sensitive, talented player without humiliation. Correct diagnosis and intervention win the stage.
key_concepts: Bobby Knight was incapable of accepting failure; every defeat was personal because coaching gave him his identity.
Knight had a fixed mindset about himself and his coaching ability, so his team had to prove his ability every time out.
Knight motivated players through intimidation and fear of his judgments and explosions.
Knight's demeaning of Daryl Thomas and the Tampax in a player's locker came from the fixed mindset.
Knight's Holy Grail was the mistake-free game, which made mistakes intolerable.
Intimidation sometimes worked, Knight had three championship teams, but at other times players and the team broke down.
In the "season on the brink," the team collapsed at the end of the season, and players escaped by transferring, breaking rules, or going early to the pros.
Steve Alford could use Knight's basketball wisdom but described the poisonous atmosphere drowning his love of the game.
Knight never seemed to analyze his motivational strategies when they were not working, never asking whether a player like Daryl Thomas needed another kind of incentive besides ridicule.

Isiah Thomas said there were times he wanted to shoot Knight and other times he wanted to hug him, and Dweck says she would not count as an unqualified success if her best student had considered shooting her.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the fixed-mindset coach: Knight's motivation through intimidation and his demand for mistake-free games flow from a fixed mindset about his own coaching identity, making every loss a personal verdict. Dweck notes the approach can win championships but also produces player breakdown, escape, and lost love of the game.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests whether you can recognize the fixed mindset operating inside a highly successful coach: Knight genuinely believed his players could develop, but his fixed mindset about himself made every loss a personal failure, so he motivated through judgment and intimidation and demanded mistake-free games.
assets.stage_1_observation: After a loss, the locker room door swings open and you watch Coach Knight single out Daryl Thomas and berate him in front of the team. The next day a Tampax appears in a player's locker. Steve Alford says the atmosphere is poisonous and that Coach's Holy Grail is the mistake-free game.
assets.stage_1_question: Why does Knight explode at his own players after a defeat, according to John Feinstein's account in the book?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Because Knight was incapable of accepting failure: every defeat was personal, the team he had selected and coached was his product and proved his ability, so a loss obliterated his identity and he judged the players who let him down.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The season collapses and players sit around fantasizing about the schools they should have chosen. You must advise a young assistant coach on how to reach a sensitive, talented player like Daryl Thomas. Knight's methods, the humiliation, the locker gift, and the jersey yank, have broken the player down on the basketball court. Choose the intervention.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Give the player honest, respectful, process-focused coaching instead of humiliation: separate the performance from the person, analyze what went wrong in terms of effort and preparation, and build a plan for improvement. The chapter shows Knight never analyzed his motivational strategies when they failed, never asking whether a player like Thomas needed a different incentive besides ridicule, so the growth-minded alternative is to diagnose and teach rather than to judge and punish.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Boss Battle: John Wooden and Full Effort Coaching
assets.visual_frame_description: The scene is the B.O. Barn, UCLA's crowded, dark, poorly ventilated practice gym in Wooden's early years. Practice has barely begun when players start coasting through drills. Coach Wooden stops, switches off the lights, and says, "Gentlemen, practice is over." Across the court, a recruit Wooden privately thought would never contribute is getting the same coaching as a future star.
assets.player_mission: Defeat the growth-minded boss scenario by first identifying what Wooden demanded from his players, then choosing the right move after he pulls Fred Slaughter in the national championship game. Correct identification and intervention win the stage.
key_concepts: John Wooden led UCLA to ten NCAA championships and an eighty-eight-game winning streak.
Wooden's rule: apply yourself each day to becoming a little better, and over time you will become a lot better.
Wooden did not ask for mistake-free games; he asked for full preparation and full effort.
Wooden's correct question was "Did I make my best effort?", and if so, "You may be outscored but you will never lose."
Wooden did not tolerate coasting; when players coasted in practice he turned out the lights and said, "Gentlemen, practice is over."
Wooden gave equal time and attention to all players regardless of initial skill, and his unheralded recruits became starters.
Wooden refused to have any player's number retired because the jersey and the number never belong to just one single player.
When Wooden pulled Fred Slaughter in the championship game, Fred understood and said he was disappointed but not upset, and was happy for Doug.
Wooden's philosophy: "For me, concern, compassion, and consideration were always priorities of the highest order."
Wooden was average in basketball tactics but exceptional at analyzing and motivating players, preparing them for life as well as basketball.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the growth-minded coaching principle that effort and preparation, not mistake-free perfection, are the measure of a player and the guarantee of development. Dweck contrasts Wooden's full preparation and full effort and his equal treatment of all players with the fixed coach's demand for mistake-free games, noting that Wooden's players credited him with preparing them for life.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests the growth-minded coaching alternative: John Wooden's rule was to apply yourself each day to becoming a little better, to demand full preparation and full effort rather than mistake-free games, and to give all players equal coaching regardless of initial talent.
assets.stage_1_observation: Practice has barely begun when the players start coasting through drills. Coach Wooden stops, switches off the lights, and says, "Gentlemen, practice is over." Later you watch him give equal time to two unheralded recruits he privately thought would never contribute, both of whom become starters.
assets.stage_1_question: What was John Wooden's coaching Holy Grail, the thing he demanded from his players?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Full preparation and full effort. Wooden rejected the question "Did I win? Did I lose?" in favor of "Did I make my best effort?", and he did not tolerate coasting because it wasted the day's opportunity to become better.
assets.stage_2_intervention: UCLA has just won its first national championship, beating Duke to finish the season thirty wins and zero losses. But Wooden is troubled: he pulled Fred Slaughter, who started every game, when the game went badly, and left in the replacement, Doug, who played well. As Wooden leaves the press conference, he heads to find Fred. You must advise Wooden's next move.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Go to Fred at once and show him that being pulled from one game does not erase his season or his worth. Wooden rushed to find Fred in the dressing room, where Fred said he understood, was disappointed but not upset, and was happy for Doug. For Wooden, concern, compassion, and consideration were always priorities of the highest order, and it is exactly this move that contrasts with a fixed coach like Knight, who would never have rushed to console Daryl Thomas.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: True vs. False Growth Mindset: Sorting Misunderstandings
assets.visual_frame_description: A school hallway in a district that has adopted the mindset message. Speech bubbles drift from teachers and parents: "I'm open-minded, so I have a growth mindset," "I tell my students they can do anything," and "I praised his effort all year." A three-column sorter awaits each claim.
assets.player_mission: Sort each mindset claim into the correct column: true growth mindset, false growth mindset, or fixed mindset. Classify every claim correctly to show that using growth language is not the same as embodying growth-minded deeds.
key_concepts: A growth mindset at its core is about believing people can develop their abilities.
Many people take what they like about themselves, like being open-minded or flexible, and call it a growth mindset.
Many people believe a growth mindset is only about effort, especially praising effort.
The process to be appreciated includes more than effort: hard work, trying new strategies, and seeking input from others.
We should never praise a process that is not there; the first question when effort praise fails is whether the child actually tried hard.
Effort praise used as a consolation prize when kids are not learning is a concern of even greater concern to Dweck than praise of absent effort.
A growth mindset does not mean telling kids they can do anything without helping them gain the skills and resources to make progress.
Blaming kids for having a fixed mindset absolves adults of responsibility for creating growth-minded environments.
In truth we are all a mixture of fixed and growth mindsets, and the task is to understand what triggers the fixed mindset.
Adults' mindsets are in their heads and are not directly visible to children; overt actions speak far louder and are what children pick up on.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix sorts mindset claims into true growth mindset, false growth mindset, and fixed mindset, testing the chapter's catalogue of misunderstandings: equating open-mindedness with growth, reducing growth to effort, praising effort as a consolation prize, and empty "you can do anything" proclamations. Dweck argues that genuine growth-mindedness is passed on through deeds, process praise tied to learning, treating setbacks as opportunities, and teaching for understanding, not through a belief sitting in an adult's head.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: Principal Osei overhears a teacher say, "I've always had a growth mindset. I always tell my students, You can do anything!" In which column does this statement belong?
assets.column_a_label: True growth mindset (developing abilities through hard work, new strategies, and help)
assets.column_b_label: False growth mindset (a misunderstanding that borrows the growth language)
assets.column_c_label: Fixed mindset (traits are permanent and are being judged)

rows.label: "You can do anything!" said with no skills, strategies, or resources offered.
"I praise my child's effort but it's not working," when the child was not really trying.
Effort praise handed out as a consolation prize to a child who tried hard but is not learning.
"I won because I have talent, therefore I will keep winning."
Calling yourself open-minded or flexible and treating that as having a growth mindset.
"Show me what you've done, let's try to understand how you're thinking, then let's figure out what you should try next."

distractors: It belongs in the fixed column because it labels children as permanently capable.
It belongs in the true growth column because it expresses strong belief in children's potential.
It belongs in no column because any talk of growth is automatically effective.
assets.explanation: The "you can do anything" proclamation is a false growth mindset: belief in children's potential only helps when adults give them the skills and resources to make progress, and otherwise it is an empty reassurance that puts the onus on the student. The false-growth category also covers calling flexibility a growth mindset, praising effort that is not there, effort praise as a consolation prize, and process praise tied to no outcome. "I won because I have talent" is a fixed-mindset attribution, while "show me what you've done, let's understand how you're thinking" is genuine growth-minded teaching for understanding.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen collage of three households: a father holding a picture of an ideal son while his teenage boy looks away, a high school senior being groomed toward one university, and a young tennis star standing beside a smiling parent. A three-column sorter labels each scene.
assets.player_mission: Sort each parental behavior into the correct column: growth-minded ideal, fixed-mindset ideal, or conditional love. Classify every scene correctly to distinguish a mold a child can never fit from love granted only on the parent's terms.
key_concepts: Fixed-mindset students described ideals that could not be worked toward, like the ideal student who comes in with innate talent.
These fixed ideals disrupted students' thinking, made them procrastinate and give up, and stressed them out because they could never measure up.
Growth-minded students described ideals like expanding their knowledge and ways of thinking, with grades as a means to continue to grow.
Growth-minded students felt they were working toward their ideal and found it inspiring.
A fixed-mindset ideal asks children to fit the mold of the brilliant, talented child or be deemed unworthy, with no room for error or for their individuality.
Nicholas felt his father compared him to a picture of an ideal son and was deeply disappointed, a message that leaked out in tone, words, and silence and left a permanent feeling of failure.
Sandy's parents wanted the label of a Harvard admission, not learning, and her record filled with A's and F's after she failed to get in.
Mark's parents refused to let him attend Stuyvesant High School because they had heard it was hard to get into Harvard from there.
John McEnroe's father lived for his son's junior career, and McEnroe says he never felt he loved tennis the way other athletes truly love their sport.
Tiger Woods's father was ambitious but made being a good person the goal: "If Tiger had wanted to be a plumber, I wouldn't have minded, as long as he was a hell of a plumber."
assets.theory_summary: This matrix sorts parental ideals and love messages into growth-minded ideals, fixed-mindset ideals, and conditional love, distinguishing a mold a child can never fit from love granted only on the parent's terms. Dweck contrasts fixed-minded parents like McEnroe's father and Sandy's Harvard-obsessed parents with Tiger Woods's father, who made being a good person the goal and left his son's love of the sport free to grow.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: In Ginott's account, seventeen-year-old Nicholas says, "In my father's mind there is a picture of an ideal son. When he compares him to me, he is deeply disappointed." To which column does Nicholas's father's ideal belong?
assets.column_a_label: Growth-minded ideal (something to strive toward and grow into)
assets.column_b_label: Fixed-mindset ideal (an innate-talent mold you either fit or not)
assets.column_c_label: Conditional love (we love you only if you succeed on our terms)

rows.label: The ideal successful student "comes in with innate talent" (fixed-mindset college students).
A successful student "whose primary goal is to expand their knowledge and their ways of thinking" (growth-minded students).
Sandy's parents: "We will love and respect you only if you go to Harvard."
McEnroe's father lived for his son's junior career, and his love depended on the success he craved.
John McEnroe says he never truly felt he loved tennis the way other athletes love their sport.
Growth-minded parents say, "I am amazed at the incredible person my child has become."

distractors: It belongs in the growth column because the father had high hopes for Nicholas.
It belongs in the conditional-love column because the father loved Nicholas.
It belongs in no column because ideals are always helpful to children.
assets.explanation: Nicholas's father held a fixed-mindset ideal, a picture of an ideal son that Nicholas could not live up to, revealed in his tone, his words, and his silence, and it left a permanent feeling of failure. Fixed-mindset ideals are things you either have or you don't, and they demoralize rather than guide. Conditional love is the distinct message "we love you only if you succeed on my terms," seen with Sandy's Harvard-or-nothing parents and McEnroe's father, while growth-minded parents give children an ideal they can strive toward and say, "I am amazed at the incredible person my child has become."
